paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 14.9 – Alberta Rules of Court – Rule 14 (Part 3)
paragraphs.text: A separate notice of appeal must be filed for each decision that is appealed, except where (a) the appeal concerns several decisions made by the court appealed from that arise out of the same hearing, (b) the appeal concerns a substantive decision, and a ruling on costs for the same hearing, (c) the appeal is of a decision that varies, confirms, explains, or provides for the enforcement of a previous decision, and the previous decision is also being appealed, or (d) a case management officer otherwise orders. Alta. Reg. 41/2014, s. 4

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 14.9:1 Rule 14.9 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 14.9. 1. Is Leave Still Required when Separate Notices of Appeal for Merits and Costs are Filed? In Brown v. Silvera, 2011 ABCA 88, 2011 CarswellAlta 382, 505 A.R. 168, 44 Alta. L.R. (5th) 221, 6 C.P.C. (7th) 36, 95 R.F.L. (6th) 320, 522 W.A.C. 168, a trial on the merits of the litigation resulted in written reasons in favour of the plaintiff being issued on September 15, 2009. A formal judgment was entered on September 18, 2009. As to the matter of costs, the direction was that “if the parties are unable to agree to costs within 2 months of the date this judgment is rendered, they may appear before me to settle the matter.” The merits of the judgment were the subject of an appeal filed on October 2, 2009 (Appeal 0903-0283AC). On January 26, 2010, the matter of costs was argued before the trial judge. She granted costs in reasons issued on April 6, 2010, but the formal judgment on costs was not entered at that point. On December 1, 2010, the appeal on the merits of the trial decision was heard by the Court of Appeal, and the Court's decision was reserved. On December15, 2010, an application was brought to settle the form of the costs judgment, and the formal judgment on costs was entered on January 5, 2011. On January 25, 2011, a second notice of appeal (relating to costs) was filed (Appeal 1103-0020AC). On March 3, 2011, the respondent brought an application to strike out the costs appeal on the ground that leave to appeal costs had not been obtained pursuant to Rule 505(3). Slatter, J.A. held that leave was not required. His Lordship, while noting the direction contained in R. 505(3), said, at paragraphs 8–15: [8] The rules also provide that a separate notice of appeal should be filed for each judgment or order that is under appeal, excepting that if a decision on the merits and a decision on costs are both being appealed, they can be appealed using the same notice of appeal: 506(3) Except as ordered by the court in exceptional circumstances, a separate notice of appeal must be filed for each order being appealed, unless those orders were granted by the same judge in the same suit (or, if applicable, consolidated suit) and arise out of the same hearing. (4) A substantive order and a later order awarding or concerning costs of the earlier substantive order shall be deemed to arise out of the same hearing. This latter rule obviously assumes that the substantive order and the costs order will be granted within a reasonable time of each other, so that the entire appeal can proceed together. [9] Where separate judgments are given on the merits and on costs, the potential appellant has two options. The first option is to file one notice of appeal for both judgments. If the costs judgment is issued before the time for appealing the merits judgment has expired, one notice of appeal can include both the judgments: R. 506(4). That notice of appeal can cover a prior costs ruling, even if the formal costs judgment has not been entered, because an appeal can be filed in anticipation of the formal judgment. If to stop time running the appeal from the merits judgment has to be filed before the costs judgment is rendered, the appellant can still apply to amend that notice of appeal to add a reference to the subsequent judgment on costs. But if no amendment is made to refer to the costs judgment, it will be assumed that the appeal is from the merits judgment only: Mahe v. Boulianne, 2010 ABCA 74, 21 Alta. L.R. (5th) 277 at para. 3. [10] In the present case the merits appeal has already been argued and reserved. While it is still theoretically possible to amend the merits notice of appeal to include an appeal from the cost judgment, that would raise several practical and procedural problems. [11] The second option available to the potential appellant is to file a second, separate notice of appeal with respect to costs. In the present case, given that the merits appeal had already been argued and reserved before the costs judgment was entered, this may have been the most practical alternative open. The present problem arose because of the undue delay in settling the terms of the costs judgment. [12] The issue on this application is whether an appellant who takes the second option (separate notices of appeal) must still obtain leave to appeal, because the separate notice of appeal respecting costs is with respect to “costs only”. The law is clear that where the appellant appeals both the merits and costs, leave is not required: Hongkong Bank of Canada v. Wheeler Holdings Ltd., [1993] 1 S.C.R. 167 at p. 210. The rationale for the rule is said to be the screening out of hopeless appeals on the issue of costs that consume an unreasonable amount of court resources. Where the appeal on the merits and the appeal and costs can be heard together, those considerations do not prevail, so no leave is required, for example, to cross-appeal costs, when the merits have already been appealed: Colborne Capital Corp. v. 542775 Alberta Ltd. (1996), 38 Alta. L.R. (3d) 127, 184 A.R. 63. [13] If this case had followed a more normal course, filing a separate notice of appeal from a separate costs judgment would have been no impediment to an appeal. If the judgment on the merits and the judgment on costs had been entered in close proximity, and the appellant nevertheless decided to file a separate appeal on each, the separate appeal on costs would not be regarded as an appeal as to “costs only”. The intent of R. 506(4) is that they be treated as one. If the appeals from the two judgments had been launched together, there would be no need for leave, and it would be merely formalistic to require leave just because separate pieces of paper had been used. [14] This appeal is distinguishable from Mahe v. Boulianne, because in that case the appellant neither amended the notice of appeal to cover the costs award, nor was a separate appeal filed. It is also distinguishable from Colborne Capital because the merits appeal and the costs appeal will not proceed contemporaneously, as the rule appears to anticipate. There does not appear to be an Alberta case on exactly the same facts. There are several cases from British Columbia that are more or less similar, but the results in them are difficult to reconcile and appear to depend on the particular facts in each: Heppner v. Schmand (1997), 29 B.C.L.R. (3d) 128; Webb v. Attewell (1994), 100 B.C.L.R. (2d) 135; Kapelus v. University of British Columbia, 2003 BCCA 109. British Columbia does not appear to have a provision like Alberta R. 506(4). [15] In my view this application depends on its unique facts. The rules simply do not contemplate a situation like this, where the appeal from the merits judgment is well underway before the costs judgment is even entered. The problem has undoubtedly risen from the delays in entering the costs judgment, for which the parties must take some responsibility. If, however, the matter had proceeded in a more regular fashion, the two appeals could have been heard together (either by amending the first notice of appeal, or by directing consolidation). In that event, no leave to appeal would have been required, because considered overall there would be no appeal as to “costs only”. In the unique circumstances of this case, and giving the appellant to the benefit of the uncertainty in the rules, leave is not required. In Rensonnet v. Uttl, 2016 ABCA 316, 2016 CarswellAlta 1982, the learned trial judge issued reasons for judgment in February 2016. No determination about costs was made at that time. On June 16, 2016, the Court of Appeal heard Uttl's appeal on the merits of the trial decision, and on June 24, 2016 dismissed that appeal. The learned trial judge heard submissions on costs on June 23, 2016, and on that day ordered each party to bear his or her own costs. Justice S. Martin of the Court of Appeal said (at paragraph 9): “… This meant that this court [the Court of Appeal] heard an appeal on the merits before the trial judge's cost decision.” Her Ladyship then said (at paragraphs 11–13): 11 As I stated at the outset of this decision, Ms. Rensonnet does not require permission to appeal the costs portion of the trial judge's decision. She has the right to appeal that decision. 12 Rule 14.5(1)(e), Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 124/2010, requires that an applicant obtain permission to appeal any decision “as to costs only”. This case does not involve an appeal “as to costs only”. The applicant was unable to file a cross-appeal with respect to costs at the time of the original appeal on the merits, given that costs had yet to be determined. As well, the appeal is not converted to one of “costs only” because the other aspects of the subsequent appeal were not permitted to go forward. 13 This situation is similar to another application brought before this court in Brown v Silvera, 2011 ABCA 88, 505 AR 168. In Brown, this court heard an appeal on the merits before the parties determined the final form of order on costs at trial. Slatter J.A. found that the costs appeal was not truly an appeal “as to costs only” because the appeals would have been heard together if the case had followed a more normal course. The applicant did not require permission to appeal the costs award. 2. When One May Combine Applications to Appeal In Percy v. Value Creation Inc., 2018 ABCA 189, 2018 CarswellAlta 946, the proposed appellants applied, by way of one application, for permission to appeal two orders of the Alberta Energy Regulator. The respondent in the application for permission to appeal sought to strike out the application on the ground, inter alia, that “separate appeals are required for separate orders”. Justice Slatter said: 4… While the Rules of Court anticipate a separate appeal for every order or judgment, R. 14.9 recognizes that there are some situations where it is more efficient to combine appeals together … There is, accordingly, no absolute rule that a separate application for permission to appeal must be brought for every order. Where one proposed appeal is about a substantive decision, and the other proposed appeal is about an order refusing to reconsider the first decision, there is no practical reason to insist on two appeals. There is accordingly nothing inappropriate about the form of amended application filed by the respondents.

paragraphs.text: A respondent who contends that the decision of the court appealed from should be varied must, within the time for filing an appeal or within 10 days of service of the notice of appeal, whichever is later, (a) file with the Registrar (i) a notice of cross appeal in Form AP-2, or (ii) where permission to cross appeal is required under rule 14.6(3), an application for permission to cross appeal, and (b) serve a filed copy of the notice of cross appeal or application on every other party to the appeal and cross appeal. sentences.text: Contents and format of notices of appeal and cross appeal

paragraphs.text: (1) A notice of appeal must be in Form AP-1 and a notice of cross appeal must be in Form AP-2. (2) A notice of appeal must contain the following information: (a) the parties' names, in the same order used in the style of cause in the court appealed from, with an indication of the status of each on the appeal and in the court appealed from; (b) the name and file number used in the court appealed from; (c) whether the whole or only part of the decision is appealed, and if only part is appealed, which part; (d) whether the appeal is required by these rules to be, or it is anticipated the appeal will be, managed as a fast track appeal; (e) whether the action under appeal was the subject of a restricted access order under Part 6, Division 4, or of any statutory restriction on publication; (f) the relief claimed. (3) A notice of appeal or cross appeal must include (a) where permission to appeal was required, particulars of or a copy of the order granting permission to appeal, and (b) particulars of or a copy of the judgment, order or other decision being appealed. Alta. Reg. 41/2014, s. 4

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 14.12:1 Rule 14.12 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 14.12. Purpose of Notice of Appeal In Easy Loan Corp. v. Base Mortgage & Investment Ltd., 2016 ABCA 163, 2016 CarswellAlta 990, Justice Wakeling said, at paragraphs 24–31, 33–41 (footnotes omitted): 24 In Alberta a notice of appeal serves three important but limited purposes. Other jurisdictions impose a heavier work load on a notice of appeal. 25 First, it gives notice to those adverse in interest to the appellant and both the court appealed from and the appeal court that the appellant challenges the validity of the lower court's decision and does not accept it as a final determination. The notice of appeal identifies what the appellant appeals. It also informs the public that the appellant challenges the validity of the judgment or order. The appellant is under no obligation to serve this second group with its notice of appeal. It must, of course, serve those adverse in interest and file the notice of appeal in both courts. 26 There is, arguably, a relationship between this function of a notice of appeal and the three objectives of reasons for judgment—enhancement of the decision-making process, promotion of effective appellate review and public accountability. In effect, the notice of appeal is the initial step in the process leading up to the framing of the issues that the appeal court will be asked to resolve on a rational basis. Because the notice of appeal is the initial step in the appeal process, it need convey minimal information. 27 Second, the notice of appeal discloses to adverse parties, the general public, the court appealed from and the appeal court the appellant's claim that the appeal court has the jurisdiction to hear its appeal challenging the validity of the decision under appeal and grant the appellant the relief it seeks. 28 This second function is not merely informative, but jurisdictional. A statutory court cannot grant remedies that are not available in law merely because they may seem convenient or helpful. 29 Third, a notice of appeal reveals to the other party and the appeal court the relief the appellant is seeking at the time the notice of appeal is filed. 30 To my mind, the third purpose is the least important of the three central purposes of a notice of appeal. This is, in part, attributable to the fact that, in most cases, the appellant's factum provides a more comprehensive treatment of the relief the appellant seeks. 31 The first and second purposes are far more important because they give notice to the other side and the appeal and lower courts that the appellant contests the lawfulness of the decision under appeal. The party adverse in interest that bases any future behaviour on the enforceability of the lower court's decision assumes the risk associated with the reversal of the lower court's decision. If the decision under appeal is overturned or varied, the respondent may incur the costs associated with reversing course. … 33 In Alberta a notice of appeal is not a record of the arguments that an appellant may make explaining why the decision appealed against is in error. 34 That is the purpose of the appellant's factum and oral argument. 35 A factum is the appellant's first opportunity to present the arguments that undermine the validity of the decision under appeal. Rules 14.25(1)(c) and (e) of the Alberta Rules of Court expressly require an appellant in a factum to provide “a concise statement of the grounds for appeal” and to address “the questions of law or fact raised by the appeal”. 36 Oral argument gives the appellant another opportunity to present the arguments that it believes are most likely to persuade the appeal court of the merit in its position. “There is no better time to emphasize one's best arguments and construct a framework that will support a … favourable decision. It is probably the single occasion counsel has the full court's attention and it is undoubtedly counsel's best opportunity to discuss the case with the judges”. 37 Rule 14.12(2) of the Alberta Rules of Court confirms that a notice of appeal has the three purposes that I suggest. This rule states that a notice of appeal must identify the judgment or order under appeal, the parties' names, whether the whole or only a part of the decision is appealed, and the relief claimed. These are mandatory elements of a notice of appeal. 38 By implication, some features of Form AP-1 are not essential features of a notice of appeal. This is because they are not cited in r. 14.12(2) of the Alberta Rules of Court. An applicant who does not provide the neutral citation of the reasons for decision under appeal and a brief description of the issues or fails to indicate whether an application will be made to expedite this appeal or the appellant believes that judicial dispute resolution is appropriate has not caused his notice of appeal to lose its status as a notice of appeal. 39 Rule 511 of the old Alberta Rules of Court demanded even less of a notice of appeal. It stipulated that a “notice of appeal shall state whether the whole or a specified part only of the judgment, order, direction, finding, verdict or award is complained of”. The need to state grounds of appeal was repealed in 1974. 40 This Court, in 599291 Alberta Ltd v Luff, opined that a “civil notice of appeal does not give grounds of appeal, and what it says about issues is merely for administrative guidance of the Court. The appellant's factum can raise issues not listed in the notice of appeal”. Generally an appellant's factum may forward any legal argument that the appellant believes supports its appeal. 41 I am satisfied that the new appeal rules introduced by the Alberta Rules of Court Amendment Regulation, 2014, effective September 1, 2014, have not altered the law in this respect. An appellant's factum may advance any argument to support an appeal provided that doing so does not contravene any governing appeal principle, such as the general prohibition against raising new issues on appeal that may prejudice other parties if a different factual base may be required to fully address the merits of the new argument.

26 There is, arguably, a relationship between this function of a notice of appeal and the three objectives of reasons for judgment—enhancement of the decision-making process, promotion of effective appellate review and public accountability.
In effect, the notice of appeal is the initial step in the process leading up to the framing of the issues that the appeal court will be asked to resolve on a rational basis.
Because the notice of appeal is the initial step in the appeal process, it need convey minimal information.

27 Second, the notice of appeal discloses to adverse parties, the general public, the court appealed from and the appeal court the appellant's claim that the appeal court has the jurisdiction to hear its appeal challenging the validity of the decision under appeal and grant the appellant the relief it seeks.
28 This second function is not merely informative, but jurisdictional.
A statutory court cannot grant remedies that are not available in law merely because they may seem convenient or helpful.
29 Third, a notice of appeal reveals to the other party and the appeal court the relief the appellant is seeking at the time the notice of appeal is filed.
30 To my mind, the third purpose is the least important of the three central purposes of a notice of appeal.
This is, in part, attributable to the fact that, in most cases, the appellant's factum provides a more comprehensive treatment of the relief the appellant seeks.

31 The first and second purposes are far more important because they give notice to the other side and the appeal and lower courts that the appellant contests the lawfulness of the decision under appeal.
The party adverse in interest that bases any future behaviour on the enforceability of the lower court's decision assumes the risk associated with the reversal of the lower court's decision.

If the decision under appeal is overturned or varied, the respondent may incur the costs associated with reversing course. … 33 In Alberta a notice of appeal is not a record of the arguments that an appellant may make explaining why the decision appealed against is in error.
34 That is the purpose of the appellant's factum and oral argument.
35 A factum is the appellant's first opportunity to present the arguments that undermine the validity of the decision under appeal.

Rules 14.25(1)(c) and (e) of the Alberta Rules of Court expressly require an appellant in a factum to provide “a concise statement of the grounds for appeal” and to address “the questions of law or fact raised by the appeal”.

36 Oral argument gives the appellant another opportunity to present the arguments that it believes are most likely to persuade the appeal court of the merit in its position. “There is no better time to emphasize one's best arguments and construct a framework that will support a … favourable decision.
It is probably the single occasion counsel has the full court's attention and it is undoubtedly counsel's best opportunity to discuss the case with the judges”.
37 Rule 14.12(2) of the Alberta Rules of Court confirms that a notice of appeal has the three purposes that I suggest.
This rule states that a notice of appeal must identify the judgment or order under appeal, the parties' names, whether the whole or only a part of the decision is appealed, and the relief claimed.
These are mandatory elements of a notice of appeal.
38 By implication, some features of Form AP-1 are not essential features of a notice of appeal.
This is because they are not cited in r.
14.12(2) of the Alberta Rules of Court.

An applicant who does not provide the neutral citation of the reasons for decision under appeal and a brief description of the issues or fails to indicate whether an application will be made to expedite this appeal or the appellant believes that judicial dispute resolution is appropriate has not caused his notice of appeal to lose its status as a notice of appeal.
39 Rule 511 of the old Alberta Rules of Court demanded even less of a notice of appeal.
It stipulated that a “notice of appeal shall state whether the whole or a specified part only of the judgment, order, direction, finding, verdict or award is complained of”.
The need to state grounds of appeal was repealed in 1974.
40 This Court, in 599291 Alberta Ltd v Luff, opined that a “civil notice of appeal does not give grounds of appeal, and what it says about issues is merely for administrative guidance of the Court.
The appellant's factum can raise issues not listed in the notice of appeal”.
Generally an appellant's factum may forward any legal argument that the appellant believes supports its appeal.
41 I am satisfied that the new appeal rules introduced by the Alberta Rules of Court Amendment Regulation, 2014, effective September 1, 2014, have not altered the law in this respect.

An appellant's factum may advance any argument to support an appeal provided that doing so does not contravene any governing appeal principle, such as the general prohibition against raising new issues on appeal that may prejudice other parties if a different factual base may be required to fully address the merits of the new argument.

sentences.text: Fast track appeals

paragraphs.text: (1) Fast track appeals are appeals from a decision, or part of a decision, that does not finally determine all or some significant part of the substantive rights in issue. (2) Unless otherwise ordered, appeals from the following kinds of decisions are to be dealt with as fast track appeals: (a) a ruling by a judge made during a trial; (b) a decision as to custody, access, guardianship, parenting time, decision-making responsibility, contact or support in respect of a child; (c) a decision concerning support for a present or former spouse or adult interdependent partner made without a trial being held; (d) a decision concerning only costs or liability to pay fees or costs; (e) a decision denying summary judgment. (3) Unless otherwise ordered, appeals from the following kinds of decisions are not fast track appeals: (a) a decision granting summary judgment or striking out a statement of claim, statement of defence or third party claim; (b) a decision refusing to open a default judgment or a noting in default; (c) a decision permitting or directing default judgment; (d) a decision staying an action indefinitely; (e) a decision dismissing an action on procedural grounds; (f) certification of or failure to certify a class proceeding. paragraphs.text: 14.18. Contents of Appeal Record—standard appeals
paragraphs.heading: Part 14. Appeals

sentences.text: Contents of Appeal Record—standard appeals

paragraphs.text: (1) The Appeal Record must meet the requirements of rule 14.21 and must contain the following: (a) a Table of Contents for Parts 1 and 2, which must list separately each document and show the page number where the document can be found; (b) Part 1—Pleadings, which must contain the relevant pleadings in the action in chronological order, including (i) the relevant pleadings, but the last version only of any pleading that was amended before trial, (ii) any amendments to pleadings made at trial, and (iii) if the appeal concerns a decision arising from an application, a copy of the application; (c) Part 2—Final Documents, which must include (i) the written or transcribed reasons (A) that led to the decision being appealed, including the reasons for any decision rendered during the trial that is relevant to the disposition of the appeal, and (B) of any prior decision of a judge, applications judge or tribunal that led to the decision now appealed, (ii) the formal judgment, order or decision appealed, (iii) any restricted access order, (iv) any prior order, reference to which is required to resolve the appeal, (v) the order granting permission to appeal, if any, (vi) the notice of appeal, (vii) the notice of cross appeal, if any, (viii) when an enactment or these rules requires service on the Minister or the Minister of Justice and Attorney General for Canada, or both, proof of that service, and (ix) if there is no oral record that can be transcribed for Part 3, a notation to that effect in the Table of Contents. (d) Part 3—Transcripts, which must contain the following information: (i) a table of contents, listing separately each part of the transcript, the name of each witness and questioner and showing the page number where the part or the testimony of the witness or questioner begins; (ii) all transcripts required by rule 14.15(1)(b); (iii) in the case of an appeal from a judgment in a jury trial, the answers given to any questions from the jury, the judge's charge to the jury and the address to the jury of each party; (iv) a list and description of all the exhibits entered in the trial court and the page in the transcripts where the entry of the exhibit is shown. (2) Where any document required for the Appeal Record is not available at the time of its preparation, a note to that effect must be inserted in the Appeal Record in its place, and the unavailable document must be filed as soon as possible or included in or appended to another document required to be filed. (2.1) The Appeal Record must not contain any comment, argument, trial briefs, legal authorities, evidence, affidavits, exhibits or new evidence. (3) A case management officer may set or vary the contents or format of the Appeal Record as the nature of the appeal requires, including giving directions respecting transcripts. Alta. paragraphs.text: Commentary § 14.18:1 Rule 14.18 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 14.18. Rule 14.90 sets out the sanctions for failure to comply with the Appeal Record rules (amongst others). The following cases were decided under the previous appeal rules, but they contain helpful guidance as to how matters should be set out in an Appeal Record. Ignoring this rule may result in no costs. However, it appears to us that the appellants should get no costs of the big appeal book filed on the main appeal. It was unfortunately prepared with little regard to r. 530(4), (6), (7), (10) on contents of appeal books. The entire events of a three-day trial are shown in the table of contents and headings as a single item. The hundreds of documents in evidence are (a) lumped together as only four items in the table of contents and headings, (b) not chronologically arranged, (c) often very repetitive, and (d) sometimes poorly reproduced, even totally illegible. One cannot make head or tail of the book unless one first spends a day preparing the chronological table which should have been found in the first few pages in the book. Those flaws greatly extended the time taken before, during, and after the hearing. Argentia Beach (Summer Village) v. Warshawski (1990), 105 A.R. 35 at 41 (C.A.). And the Court of Appeal further said: The appeal book violates rule 530(4), (6) by twice treating each affidavit and its bulky exhibits as a single item. We have criticized such flaws in a number of reported judgments, and in some reduced costs as a result. The time for awarding full costs for such defective appeal books may not last much longer. Brown v. Northey (1991), 115 A.R. 321 at 324 (C.A.). Similarly: The appeal book here is very hard to use. Contrary to R. 530(6), the 84 exhibits are simply lumped in with affidavits. They are not listed separately, let alone reproduced in chronological order. Some of the plaintiff's exhibits contain dozens of letters in one bundle. Reading a few letters at random or by selection does not give a proper picture of the events in the suit. The picture described above emerges only after one makes a list of exhibits with dates, and then reads them all in chronological order … We would disallow two thirds of the disbursements for the appeal book because of the breach of R. 530(6). Taylor Estate v. McArthur (1990), 72 Alta. L.R. (2d) 202 at 204, 206 (C.A.). Similarily: The appeal books follow an annoying practice. They lump together a whole binder of documents, hundreds of pages long, as a single item in the book and in its table of contents. When one looks for a document which is in the midst of one of those, finding it is almost impossible. The appeal books also omit the first page of the critical consent order recited above. In one or two places, the reasons for judgment referred to in the agreement as to contents is not that found in the corresponding part of the book. That is slipshod preparation. Had Kredl [appellant] won (which he did not), he would probably have not got any costs for those portions of the appeal book. Calmont Leasing Ltd. v. Kredl (1995), 30 Alta. L.R. (3d) 16 (C.A.), at 30, per curiam. 1. Obtain Reasons for Judgment We do not have the benefit of the reasons of the trial judge, although we were advised, during the argument, of some of the reasoning. This is but another occasion when we regret not having the reasons available. Although a reporter was not present, the learned chambers judge, if he had been asked, might have been able to provide a memorandum, make a note or memorandum on the record, or call in a reporter. We take this occasion to suggest to counsel that they might ask for some record in appropriate cases. It is particularly important for us to know when material that is not on the record has been put forward, what concessions were made, and what points were argued. It is very helpful to have the precise basis for the decision. Melsness v. Alberta (Minister of Social Services & Community Health) (1982), 18 Alta. L.R. (2d) 314 at 317 (C.A.). The Court of Appeal has repeated the request for copies of the reasons of the court from which the appeal is taken: Counsel for the appellant filed the Chambers Judge's reasons late. He suggested that only recently had the Court of Appeal indicated that it wanted any recorded reasons transcribed. That is not so. For at least a decade we have been urging counsel to arrange to have reasons for decision recorded in the first instance. Since time immemorial, the Court has expected an appellant to have any recorded reasons for the decision transcribed for the appeal. South Calgary Properties Ltd. v. J.T. Miller Construction Ltd. (1995), 29 Alta. L.R. (3d) 393, at 399, per curiam. In Alberta (Provincial Court Judge) v. Alberta (Provincial Court Chief Judge) (2007), (sub nom. Reilly, P.C.J. v. Walter, C.J.P.C.) 404 A.R. 1 (Alta. C.A.), Hunt J.A. reaffirmed that the reasons of the judge appealed from should be included in the appeal book, but that argument generally should not be included. At pp. 2–3, her Ladyship said: 4 The Rules of Court provide that only material that is “truly necessary” to the appeal should be included in appeal books: Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 390/68, R. 530(14). 5 It is well-recognized in civil cases that if reasons are available, the transcript of argument ought not generally to be included in the appeal books, if one party objects. W.A. Stevenson & J.E. Côté, Alberta Civil Procedure Handbook 2007, vol. 1 (Edmonton: Juriliber, 2007) at 550. The rationale for excluding comments by a judge during argument has been expressed in this way: During the hearing of an appeal Viscount Simon L.C., referring to reports which might be made of the case, said that it was well understood that interlocutory observations of members of the Board or of a Court were not judicial pronouncements. They did not decide anything, even provisionally. They were made to elucidate the argument, to point the question, or to indicate what were the matters which the judicial spokesman thought needed to be investigated, and that was all. It would bea very great pity, and a profound error, if anybody, foreigner or fellow-subject, supposed that interlocutory observations were anything more. Faryna v. Chorney, [1952] 2 D.L.R. 354 at para. 7 (B.C.C.A.), approved in R. v. Hodson, [2001] A.J. No. 601, 2001 ABCA 111 at paras. 33–35. 6 I see no reason to depart from that sound principle in this case. I have reviewed the decision under appeal as well as the parts of the transcript submitted with the application and those handed to me during oral argument. Based on that review, I am satisfied that there is nothing in the comments of the chambers judge during argument that adds to, detracts from, or sheds light on her subsequent decision, which was apparently written after she had reviewed in detail the extensive authorities submitted to her, as well as the material forming the record. 7 Such extraneous material makes the appeal record unnecessarily bulky and adds to costs. It could also inhibit the free exchange of ideas between the judge and counsel during argument. 8 Obviously, there are cases that fall outside the scope of this general approach (for example, when the transcript itself reveals the reasons for the decision). But this is not such a case. 2. Include Neither Too Much Nor Too Little in Appeal Book The appeal books provided to us contain no record of the evidence adduced at trial or of the argument made in relation to the trial judge's ruling on the non-suit application. While we commend counsel for deleting irrelevant material from the appeal books, here such zealous pruning leaves us with a scanty record containing no factual background which would ordinarily be essential to understand the non-suit argument. R. v. ASL Paving Ltd. (1995), 28 Alta. L.R. (3d) 38 (C.A.), at 40, per curiam.

The rationale for excluding comments by a judge during argument has been expressed in this way: During the hearing of an appeal Viscount Simon L.C., referring to reports which might be made of the case, said that it was well understood that interlocutory observations of members of the Board or of a Court were not judicial pronouncements.
They did not decide anything, even provisionally.
They were made to elucidate the argument, to point the question, or to indicate what were the matters which the judicial spokesman thought needed to be investigated, and that was all.
It would bea very great pity, and a profound error, if anybody, foreigner or fellow-subject, supposed that interlocutory observations were anything more.
Faryna v.
Chorney, [1952] 2 D.L.R.
354 at para.
7 (B.C.C.A.), approved in R. v.
Hodson, [2001] A.J.
No.
601, 2001 ABCA 111 at paras.
6 I see no reason to depart from that sound principle in this case.
I have reviewed the decision under appeal as well as the parts of the transcript submitted with the application and those handed to me during oral argument.

Based on that review, I am satisfied that there is nothing in the comments of the chambers judge during argument that adds to, detracts from, or sheds light on her subsequent decision, which was apparently written after she had reviewed in detail the extensive authorities submitted to her, as well as the material forming the record.
7 Such extraneous material makes the appeal record unnecessarily bulky and adds to costs.
It could also inhibit the free exchange of ideas between the judge and counsel during argument.
8 Obviously, there are cases that fall outside the scope of this general approach (for example, when the transcript itself reveals the reasons for the decision).
But this is not such a case.

Include Neither Too Much Nor Too Little in Appeal Book The appeal books provided to us contain no record of the evidence adduced at trial or of the argument made in relation to the trial judge's ruling on the non-suit application.

While we commend counsel for deleting irrelevant material from the appeal books, here such zealous pruning leaves us with a scanty record containing no factual background which would ordinarily be essential to understand the non-suit argument.
R. v.
ASL Paving Ltd.
L.R.
(3d) 38 (C.A.), at 40, per curiam.

paragraphs.text: (1) The appellant in a standard appeal must file an appellant's factum that meets the requirements of rules 14.25 and 14.26, and must serve a filed copy on every other party to the appeal before the earlier of (a) 2 months after the filing of the Appeal Record, and (b) 6 months after the filing of the notice of appeal or the appeal will be struck by the Registrar. paragraphs.text: Commentary § 14.25:1 Rule 14.25 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 14.25. 1. Remember to Reproduce Statutes and Regulations With the advent of books of authorities, many counsel neglect R. 540(4), which requires them to reproduce in their facta statutes or regulations, “or so much thereof as may be necessary to the decision of the case”. If all that is reproduced in the book of authorities, the omission does no harm. But if the book of authorities contains only the sections which that party directly urges in argument, the omission does harm. The court needs all the relevant sections of the statute or regulation, including those which help the opposing side, or those whose effect is admitted, or those which help both sides. High Level Investments Ltd. v. First City Trust Co. (1990), 74 Alta. L.R. (2d) 274 at 277 (C.A.). In Royal Bank of Canada v. Hallmark Golf Developments Inc. (1993), 12 Alta. L.R. (3d) 362, the Court of Appeal, at p. 367, again said: Counsel would assist the Court greatly by complying with the Rule which calls for an appendix in each factum reproducing the portions of the statutes relied upon. In R. v. Maygard, 2013 ABCA 214, 2013 CarswellAlta 986, 553 A.R. 266, the Court reminded the bar that requirement to reproduce the relevant sections of legislation includes sections of the Criminal Code. The Court said, at paragraph 49: 49 The Rules of Court call for reproduction of relevant statutes in the factums, though putting that in the book of authorities would suffice. However, counsel in criminal appeals often flatter the Court by assuming that the judges have memorized the entire Criminal Code, and so counsel do not reproduce sections from it. That is not so, and reproducing the relevant sections would speed up the administration of justice. 2. Books of Authorities The union local filed a book of authorities. Most cases cited are reported in well-known sets of law reports. But often the copies given to us were downloaded and printed from some computer service, and bore neither page numbers nor paragraph numbers. It is difficult for counsel and the court to describe to each other where to find specific passages, under such circumstances. That is doubly unfortunate when the judges sometimes need to work away from a law library. Counsel should ensure that reported cases bear either paragraph numbers, or page numbers from a law report. Wiebe v. Labour Relations Board (Alta.) (2001), 281 A.R. 362 (C.A.), at 367, per curiam. 3. Specifically Claim for Trial Costs To Avoid Uncertainty In ENMAX Energy Corporation v. Alberta, 2018 ABCA 291, 2018 CarswellAlta 1889, 73 Alta. L.R. (6th) 40, 2018 D.T.C. 5106, the court noted that “the respondent argues that the appellant is not entitled to costs of the trial, because trial costs were not included in the relief claimed in the appellant's factum.” The Court said: 4 It is obviously the better practice for the appellant to specify all the relief that it claims, including a specific claim for trial costs: R. 14.25(1)(f). The failure to specify a claim for trial costs if the appeal is allowed, however, is not necessarily fatal if there is no surprise or prejudice: R. 1.3(2), 1.5(4); MacPhail v Karasek, 2006 ABCA 354 at para. 6, 69 Alta LR (4th) 16, 401 AR 100. The appellant's factum asked that “the appeal be allowed with costs”, which in the circumstances of this appeal was sufficient. 4. Grounds In 1242311 Alberta Ltd. v. Tricon Developments Inc., 2021 ABCA 418, 2021 CarswellAlta 3165, the Court said: [19] The general rule is that where an issue was not raised in the pleadings or argued before the trial judge, it cannot be a ground of appeal: 681210 Alberta Ltd v Hunter, 2012 ABCA 83 at paras 25–27.

paragraphs.text: (1) Factums must be (a) formatted using at least 12 point font, one-inch margins and at least 1.5 line spacing, except for quotations, and (b) continuously paginated, with the cover page being page 1, and have electronic bookmarks as required by rule 14.87(1)(i). (3) Factums must contain precise references to the location, page numbers and paragraph numbers or lines of the Appeal Record, Extracts of Key Evidence and authorities referred to. sentences.text: Oral argument

paragraphs.text: (1) Unless otherwise directed, (a) all appeals will be set down on the Civil Appeal Hearing List for an oral hearing, and (b) the appeal and any cross appeal will be argued at the same time. (2) On agreement of all parties, or on the direction of a single appeal judge, the Court of Appeal may hear and decide an appeal without oral argument. (3) The Court of Appeal may proceed with the hearing of an appeal when scheduled, even if (a) a party does not appear at the scheduled time, or (b) any party has failed to file its factum. (4) Unless the panel otherwise permits, oral argument must not exceed 45 minutes for each separately represented party in the appeal, with any consolidated appeals to be treated as one appeal. paragraphs.text: Commentary § 14.32:1 Transcripts of Oral Argument See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 14.32. In McDonald v. Brookfield Asset Management Inc., 2016 ABCA 419, 2016 CarswellAlta 2471, the appellants requested a transcript of the oral argument which preceded the Court's decision in the main appeal. The application was dismissed. The Reasons of the Court were as follows: 1 THE COURT:—The appellant has requested a transcript of the oral argument leading to the decision reported as McDonald v Brookfield Asset Management, 2016 ABCA 375. The policy of the Court is that the digital recordings of oral argument are for internal use only, and transcripts will not be provided except in exceptional circumstances upon authorization of the panel or judge presiding at the hearing. 2 The appellant advises that he intends to seek leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada, and he requires the transcripts to: (a) confirm the ruling on the admissibility of fresh evidence, and (b) clarify the “discussion surrounding” certain issues during the oral argument, in relation to proposed arguments in support of the application for leave to appeal, i.e. that the reasons for decision overlook or incorrectly apply some of the relevant statutory wording or evidence. Neither of these is a circumstance requiring the transcripts. 3 Firstly, the reasoning of the Court is found in the Memorandum of Judgment. Any reviewable errors, and any issues of national importance justifying leave to appeal will be found in that Memorandum. If issues or evidence were overlooked, that will be apparent from a review of the Memorandum. 4 Specifically, discussions during oral argument are not a part of the reasons of the Court. The point was made by Viscount Simon, and reported in a Practice Note, [1942] WN 89: During the hearing of an appeal Viscount Simon L.C., referring to reports which might be made of the case, said that it was well understood that interlocutory observations of members of the Board or of a Court were not judicial pronouncements. They did not decide anything, even provisionally. They were made to elucidate the argument, to point the question, or to indicate what were the matters which the judicial spokesman thought needed to be investigated, and that was all. It would be a very great pity, and a profound error, if anybody, foreigner or fellow-subject, supposed that interlocutory observations were anything more. Appellate Courts have repeatedly emphasized that questions asked or opinions expressed during oral argument do not necessarily reflect the final position of that judge, much less any sort of final adjudication by the panel of the Court: Toliver v Koepke, 2013 ABCA 390 at para. 6, 566 AR 24; R. v Hehn, 2008 BCCA 170 at para. 35, 254 BCAC 215; R. v Sanghera, 2015 BCCA 326 at para. 59, 375 BCAC 78; Menzies v Harlos (1989), 37 BCLR (2d) 249, 37 CPC (2d) 94 (CA); R. v Baccari, 2011 ABCA 205 at para. 24, 510 AR 301. It follows that if there are any reviewable errors to be found, they are to be found in the Memorandum of Decision, and the transcripts of the oral argument are generally irrelevant. 5 Secondly, it is rarely necessary or appropriate for the Court to provide “clarification” of the reasons for decision. The reasons must speak for themselves, and stand or fall based on the reasoning (or absence of reasoning) in them. In those rare cases where some clarification is appropriate, the proper procedure is to apply to the panel for clarification, not for counsel to sort through the oral argument in an attempt to supplement the formal written reasons. 6 With respect specifically to the ruling on the fresh evidence application, the long standing practice of the Court is that such applications are adjourned over, and are heard by the same panel hearing the substantive appeal: R. 14.38(2)(b). That is because a part of the test for the admission of fresh evidence is whether it could, when considered with the rest of evidence, reasonably be expected to have affected the result. A consideration of the fresh evidence application therefore involves a consideration of the merits of the appeal, and it is most efficient that the application and the appeal be heard at the same time. As a result, it is possible that the panel might hear the contents of the fresh evidence during the argument of the appeal, but ultimately rule that it is inadmissible. Counsel must effectively argue the appeal on the basis that the fresh evidence will, or will not be admitted: Armoyan v Armoyan, 2013 NSCA 99 at para. 132, 334 NSR (2d) 204. 7 The procedure for having the same panel hear both the application for fresh evidence and the appeal was set out in R. v Stolar, [1988] 1 SCR 480 at pp. 491-2: The procedure which should be followed when an application is made to the Court of Appeal for the admission of fresh evidence is that the motion should be heard and, if not dismissed, judgment should be reserved and the appeal heard. In this way, the Court of Appeal has the opportunity to consider the question of fresh evidence against the whole background of the case and all the other evidence in the case. It is then in a position where it can decide realistically whether the proffered evidence could reasonably have been expected to affect the result of the case. If, then, having heard the appeal, the court should be of the opinion that the evidence could not reasonably have affected the result, it would dismiss the application for the introduction of fresh evidence and proceed to a disposition of the appeal. On the other hand, if it should be of the view that the fresh evidence is of such nature and effect that, taken with the other evidence, it would be conclusive of the issues in the case, the Court of Appeal could dispose of the matter then and there. Where, however, the fresh evidence does not possess that decisive character which would allow an immediate disposition of the appeal but, nevertheless, has sufficient weight or probative force that if accepted by the trier of fact, when considered with the other evidence in the case, it might have altered the result at trial, the Court of Appeal should admit the proffered evidence and direct a new trial where the evidence could be heard and the issues determined by the trier of fact. This was the procedure outlined by the Chief Justice at the commencement of the oral argument, and followed by the panel in this appeal. 8 When appellant's counsel asked, the panel confirmed (after the routine morning break) that he was at liberty to refer to the fresh evidence during the oral argument, on the basis that its admissibility would be considered along with the disposition of the substance of the appeal. The panel never ruled during the oral argument that the fresh evidence was admissible, and merely confirmed that it could be referred to. The fact that the evidence was subsequently ruled inadmissible is not inconsistent with permitting its use during the oral argument. As stated in Stolar at p. 487: “… there is a distinction between an order which actually admits the proffered evidence and one which allows consideration of the evidence for the purpose of determining whether it will be admitted”. 9 The draft press release of July 3, 2008 was added to the record at the oral argument on the consent of the respondents. 10 The request for release of the transcripts of the oral argument is accordingly refused.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 14.36:1 Rule 14.36 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 14.36. 1. Applications under the Rule In Kainaiwa/Blood Tribe v. Alberta (Minister of Energy), 2020 ABCA 387, 2020 CarswellAlta 2046, Alberta (Minister of Energy) asked the Court's Case Management Office to set down for hearing the appeal which had been previously adjourned. The Court's Case Management Office (CMO) refused to do so, and left the appeal adjourned pending dispositions of related court proceedings. Alberta filed an application under Rule 14.36 for a rescission of the CMO decision. Madam Justice Antonio dismissed the application and set out the approach to be taken on such applications: [18] The Blood Tribe asserts that “the CMO's decision is entitled to deference, and a reviewing judge ought not to simply rehear the matter or substitute its views over those of the case manager.” It relies on authority from British Columbia to the effect that case management decision may only be overturned for an error in principle or a misapprehension of the evidence. The authorities provided address appeals from chambers justices, masters, and administrative tribunals, respectively: 0742848 BC Ltd v 426008 BC Ltd, 2020 BCCA 179; JN Cram & Associates v Doll and Penny's Cafe Ltd, 1993 CanLII 197 (BCCA), 82 BCLR (2d) 139; Neill v British Columbia (Expropriation Compensation Board) (1996), 1996 CanLII 3196 (BC CA), 69 BCAC 119. In other words, these authorities concern appeals from judicial and quasi-judicial bodies. [19] The role of this Court's Case Management Officers is quite different. At the direction of the Court, CMOs may assist “with respect to the management of matters before the Court and the business of the Court”: Court of Appeal Act, RSA 2000, c C-30, s 14. Their authority includes, among many other things, the scheduling of hearings. CMOs communicate with the parties or their counsel, as appropriate, and manage the progress of the Court's files. The CMOs' ability to make administrative directions, and to assume that those directions will be respected, is essential to the efficient functioning of this Court. By empowering them to make administrative directions, the Legislature has placed faith in the CMOs' good judgment. [20] That said, CMOs are not members of the judiciary. Rule 14.36(3) provides an avenue by which parties may bring their procedural questions before a justice of this Court. Rule 14.36(3) does not use the words “appeal” or “review”. By contrast, rules 6.14(1), 10.26(1) and 10.44(1) respectively provide for “appeals” of decisions of masters, review officers and assessment officers. The difference in wording suggests a difference in meaning. [21] I conclude that an application under rule 14.36(3) it is not best conceived of as an “appeal”. A justice hearing an application under rule 14.36(3) will consider the question directly and make his or her own decision. That decision may wholly or partially align with or depart from the CMO's direction, such that in the result, the justice may rescind, confirm, amend or enforce it. In Okeke v. Oakes, 2024 ABCA 305, leave to appeal refused 2024 ABCA 379, Madam Justice Woolley said: [12] A justice hearing an application under Rule 14.36(3) will consider the question directly and make his or her own decision: Kainaiwa at para 21; Bruneau v Quinn, 2024 ABCA 108 at para 3. While case management officers are not owed deference in the traditional sense, a judge asked to rescind a decision of a case management officer should pay careful consideration to that decision and any reasons for it: Tallcree First Nation v Rath & Company and Rath, 2021 ABCA 360 at para 41.

By contrast, rules 6.14(1), 10.26(1) and 10.44(1) respectively provide for “appeals” of decisions of masters, review officers and assessment officers.
The difference in wording suggests a difference in meaning.
[21] I conclude that an application under rule 14.36(3) it is not best conceived of as an “appeal”.
A justice hearing an application under rule 14.36(3) will consider the question directly and make his or her own decision.
That decision may wholly or partially align with or depart from the CMO's direction, such that in the result, the justice may rescind, confirm, amend or enforce it.
In Okeke v.

Oakes, 2024 ABCA 305, leave to appeal refused 2024 ABCA 379, Madam Justice Woolley said: [12] A justice hearing an application under Rule 14.36(3) will consider the question directly and make his or her own decision: Kainaiwa at para 21
Bruneau v Quinn, 2024 ABCA 108 at para 3.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 14.37:1 Rule 14.37 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 14.37. 1. Application to Amend Notice of Appeal In Easy Loan Corp. v. Base Mortgage & Investment Ltd., 2016 ABCA 163, 2016 CarswellAlta 990, Justice Wakeling said, at paragraphs 6-7: 6 Rule 14.37(1) allows a single judge of this Court to determine whether a notice of appeal may be amended. This is an application incidental to an appeal. 7 A notice of appeal may be amended if the proposed amendment does not enlarge the scope of the appeal set out in the filed notice of appeal. 2. Extending time In Murfin v. Barnes, 2017 ABCA 441, 2017 CarswellAlta 2793, Justice Veldhuis set out the test for extending time to file an appeal. 3 In general, Rule 14.64 of the Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 124/2010 directs the Registrar to strike an appeal if the appellant has not filed the Appeal Record and factum within the required time period. However, this court may excuse compliance with deadlines and “exercise its discretion to grant the extension in any event” if “there are ‘unique and special circumstances’ and it is in the interests of justice to do so.”Stoddard v Montague, 2006 ABCA 109 (CanLII) at para 8, 412 AR 88. See also rules 1.4(2)(h) and 13.5(2). In the context of an application for an extension of time to file a factum, the pertinent factors to consider are the reason for the delay, the prospects of moving ahead with the appeal, prejudice to the other party, and the potential merit of the appeal: Keef v Peters, 2015 ABCA 16 (CanLII) at para 6, [2015] A.J. No. 24. 4 A delay in securing funding from Legal Aid Alberta due to no fault of the applicant would be a special circumstance that justifies granting an extension of time. However, the analysis does not end there. 5 An extension of time is a discretionary remedy that requires the court to weigh numerous factors and “determine if it is in the interest of justice to permit the appeal to proceed”: Prochazka v Alberta (Maintenance Enforcement Program), 2014 ABCA 448 (CanLII) at para 4, [2014] A.J. No. 1439 (QL). In Bretin v. Ross, 2017 ABCA 389, 2017 CarswellAlta 2441, Madam Justice S. Martin said: 26 The test for extension of time to appeal is well-known: Alberta Health Services v Wang, 2017 ABCA 198 at para 12. Mr. Bretin must show: 1. a bona fide intention to appeal while the right to appeal existed; 2. an explanation for the failure to appeal in time that serves to excuse or justify the lateness; 3. an absence of serious prejudice such that it would not be unjust to disturb the judgment; 4. the applicant must not have taken the benefits of the judgment under appeal; and 5. a reasonable chance of success on the appeal, which might better be described as a reasonable arguable appeal. Also see Alberta (Director of Law Enforcement) v. McPike, 2019 ABCA 330, 2019 CarswellAlta 1938, at paragraphs 15–20. “These principles are equally applicable to applications for extension of time for permission to appeal”: paragraph 20. Further, in that case, the Court said: 1. “To be bona fide, the applicant's intent must be genuine and unconditional … must have existed before the time period expired and continued until the moment of expiry …, and must have been expressed to the respondent. …”: paragraph 22. 2. “A ‘reasonable chance of success’ on an application for extension of time (and as we will see below, for an application for permission to appeal) is a low standard. It is enough if the applicant's position is arguable. A position is arguable if it is not hopeless or frivolous. …”: paragraph 41. 3. Anonymizing a name In AB v. College of Physicians and Surgeons of Alberta, 2021 ABCA 320, 2021 CarswellAlta 2337, Justice Wakeling said (footnotes omitted): [7] Rule 14.37(1) of the Alberta Rules of Court[5] states that “a single appeal judge may hear and decide any application incidental to an appeal”. A decision to anonymize a party's name is a matter “incidental to an appeal”. If a decision to anonymize a party's name is not a matter incidental to an appeal, the inherent jurisdiction of the court to administer justice fairly authorizes this order. 4. Rule 14.37(2) In Betser-Zilevitch v. Prowse Chowne LLP, 2022 ABCA 134, 2022 CarswellAlta 891, Justice Watson discussed the effect of Rule 14.37(2), and said: [19] On that question of ‘single judge’ authority, I am satisfied that Rule 14.37(2) is intended to provide specific examples covered in the larger scope of authority in Rule 14.37(1) as is intended to be granted to single judges. This purpose of subsection (2) is underscored by the fact that some of the situations listed in Rule 14.37(2) might otherwise raise a question of finality that might beg the question whether a quorum of a panel was required under s 7 of the Court of Appeal Act. More directly, s 1 of the Judicature Act defines a “Court” as “on appeal, the Court of Appeal”. Section 4 of the Judicature Act says that the “judges of the Court have … all the powers … of a judge of a superior court of record”. I hasten to clarify that I am not suggesting that single judges should exercise prerogative powers of a superior court judge under this authority read with Rule 14.37. It is part of the authority platform to be considered, however. Rather, the authority of single judges is best understood in the context of process matters: compare E(H) v Association of Professional Engineers and Geoscientists of Alberta, 2019 ABCA 298, [2019] AJ No 1052 (QL). 5. Single judge may order access restriction In Betser-Zilevitch v. Prowse Chowne LLP, 2022 ABCA 134, 2022 CarswellAlta 891, Justice Watson said, at paragraph 20: … I am satisfied that the subject matter of the application before me, which is for an access or disclosure restriction order of court records of this Court, is within the jurisdiction of a single judge. … 6. When a single judge may not grant a stay In Great North Equipment Inc. v. Penney, 2024 ABCA 378, Justice Hawkes explained when a single Court of Appeal Justice may not issue a stay. His Lordship said: [7] Single members of this Court, when sitting pursuant to the rules identified above, do not have the ability to grant a stay where the order appealed from granted no affirmative relief. To allow this stay application would be to effectively grant the remedy sought in the full appeal in advance of the appeal. The authorities preclude a stay in such circumstances: Noscenco v Bagayeva, 2015 ABCA 266 at para 7; Denis v Sauvageau, 2022 ABCA 166 at para 15; Dr Vu v College of Physicians & Surgeons of Alberta, 2023 ABCA 377 at paras 14-15, and the authorities cited therein.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 14.38:1 Rule 14.38 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 14.38. In S. (C.K.) v. S. (O.S.), 2014 ABCA 416, 2014 CarswellAlta 2205, the Court summarized, at paragraph 10, the test for the admission of new evidence at the appeal: [10] In addition to having to satisfy the familiar four requirements from the Palmer test (Palmer v The Queen, 1979 CanLII 8 (SCC), [1980] 1 SCR 759, 30 NR 181), the evidence, to be admitted as fresh evidence on appeal, must have been admissible at trial: for example, Somji v Wilson, 2014 ABCA 35 (CanLII) at para 7, [2014) AJ No 88 (QL), leave denied [2014] SCCA No 155 (QL). It should be evidence that makes a difference even if post-trial: see Ackerman v Ackerman, 2014 SKCA 86 (CanLII) at paras 18 to 22, 48 RFL 7th 1. Proposed evidence on appeal should be material, cogent and of compelling significance: R v Sipos, 2014 SCC 47 (CanLII) at para 29, 311 CCC (3d) 121. In O. (R.) v. F. (D.), 2015 ABCA 267, a self-represented appellant applied “to amend her application to the Court to introduce new evidence on appeal”. In the course of dismissing that application, but granting the appellant additional time to file a properly prepared application, the Court provided helpful comments about some of the questions to which material in support of such an application should be addressed: 12 If the appellant desires to apply for permission of the Court to introduce yet more evidence, she must file a second supplementary application consistent with Rule 14.38(2)(b) supported by (a) a proper notice of application; (b) an affidavit from herself addressing the criteria for admission of new evidence on appeal; and (c) an affidavit from the proposed new witness. The affidavit of that proposed new witness must identify what the witness proposes to provide as fresh evidence, and it must address the criteria for admission of new evidence, as well as setting out in relation to any opinion evidence what the proposed new witness is qualified to say by way of opinion evidence and why the witness is qualified to say it. 13 It seems apt to repeat the advisement to the appellant that she must understand that the standard of review for this Court is not a matter of the Court approaching any issues in her appeals in a de novo manner. This Court does not simply assume the function of the first instance court, either when composed of a single judge or a quorum panel. 14 It may be of assistance to the appellant to point out that a panel of the Court may be asked to consider, in applying the test in Palmer or otherwise, whether the proposed evidence is or would be admissible under any rules of law applicable to its nature, its source, its continuity from point of creation to point of offer in evidence and its balance of probative force against prejudicial effect. 15 The Court may be asked to consider the cogency of the evidence in the sense of its essential credibility, its relevance, its materiality to a decisive issue, and its capacity to have a real effect on any issue to which it relates. 16 The Court may be asked to consider any explanation offered for the fact that the evidence was not offered in the legally appropriate manner at the proper time earlier. 17 The Court may be asked to consider whether admission of the evidence at this time would be adjudicatively unfair or distort either the appeal process or any other proceedings. 18 The panel hearing the appeal has full discretionary authority to do what it finds to be just and appropriate on any such application. Nothing I say can limit that. 1. Matters Incidental to Appeal Determining if the appeal is plainly hopeless is not “incidental”. The respondent plaintiff contends that on the interlocutory motion, the soundness of the appeal was in issue. It is true that the grounds for that appeal were mentioned in the affidavit for time extension, and that the opposing affidavit annexed the reasons for judgment at trial. But it was no function of the chambers judge to decide that the appeal was correct. The most that he had to decide (if the point was argued), was that the appeal was not frivolous. Where such a small time extension was in issue, clearly there could be no question of refusing the time extension unless the appeal was plainly hopeless. That is a state of affairs common to many interlocutory applications. What is more, one judge of the Court of Appeal can only hear matters incidental to an appeal under R. 516. Had he been of the view that the appeal was plainly hopeless, he could not have condemned it to virtual death himself. He would have had to refer it to a panel. Stahl Diesel Sales Ltd. v. Cunningham Estate (1992), 2 Alta. L.R. (3d) 133 at 135 (C.A.). In Imperial Oil Ltd. v. Alberta (Minister of Environment) (2005), 376 A.R. 381 (C.A. [In Chambers]), Hunt J.A. considered the phrase “incidental to an appeal”. Her Ladyship said, at p. 386: In my view, the question of intervener costs following a discontinuance is incidental to an appeal. Such a decision does not determine substantive issues between the parties (such as those that would have been decided had the appeal proceeded). Putting this question before a single judge also makes sense from the point of view of judicial economy (which is one policy reason behind rule 516). When an appeal has been heard, the panel is best-situated to award costs, since its members will be familiar with the strengths and weaknesses of each side's arguments, as well as with the conduct of the case. But when an appeal has been discontinued, no judge has detailed information about it. It is logical that only one judge, and not three, expends time to resolve the issue. I conclude that a single judge has authority to determine whether interveners should be awarded the costs of a discontinued appeal. In CCS Corporation v. Pembina Pipeline Corporation, 2017 ABCA 260, 2017 CarswellAlta 1418, Justice Slatter said, at paragraph 7: 7 The scope of matters “incidental to an appeal” is not precisely defined, but it is well established that any determination of the merits of an appeal must be made by a full 3 judge panel of the Court: R. 14.38(2)(a); R. 14.74; Kohut v Wilson, 2002 ABCA 247 at para. 7; Square and Level Holdings Inc. v Manuel-Domshy, 2005 ABCA 85 at para. 13; Berthin v Berthin, 2017 BCCA 178 at para. 22. This application, in its initial form, invited a single judge to decide the merits of one of the grounds of appeal, which is beyond the mandate of a single judge. 2. Re-arguing Appeal Leave to re-argue should not be granted merely to allow counsel to make arguments that could have been made in the original hearing. Nova, An Alta. Corp. v. Guelph Engineering Co. et al. and Daniel Valve Co. et al. (1989), 71 Alta. L.R. (2d) 80 at 82 (C.A.). This court has refused to grant leave where there were no new arguments made that would affect the result of the earlier decision. White Resource Management Ltd. v. Durish, [1993] A.U.D. 1092 (C.A.). It has also refused leave where there were alleged errors of fact made by the court but where such alleged errors were not germane to the issue being dealt with. W.W. Construction (Lethbridge) Ltd. et al. v. Red Deer College (1990), 71 Alta. L.R. (2d) 396 at 398 (C.A.). Leave should be granted “if it appears that the court overlooked or misapprehended the evidence in a significant respect, and that a risk of miscarriage of justice ensued …”Menzies v. Harlos and Devlin (1989), 37 B.C.L.R. (2d) 249 at 255 (C.A.). The Supreme Court of Canada has suggested that rehearing may be appropriate if the court has misled itself or was misled as regards what was the record before it, the nature of the issues, or the questions to be addressed. Protestant School Board of Greater Montreal et al. v. Quebéc (Procureur général) et al. (1989), 97 N.R. 143 at 145 [N.R.] (S.C.C.). Arrowhead Auto & Truck Parts Ltd. v. Calgary (City) (1997), 196 A.R. 57 (C.A.), at pp. 57-58, per curiam. The above quoted excerpt was referred to with approval in H. (V.A.) v. Lynch, 2000 ABCA 213, 2000 CarswellAlta 795, 266 A.R. 150, 85 Alta. L.R. (3d) 51; additional reasons at 2001 ABCA 37, 2001 CarswellAlta 148, 277 A.R. 104, 91 Alta. L.R. (3d) 1; reconsideration refused 2001 ABCA 211, 2001 CarswellAlta 1196, 293 A.R. 395, 95 Alta. L.R. (3d) 299, at 153, per Wittmann J.A. It was also referred to with approval in Financial Management Inc. v. Associated Financial Planners Ltd. (2006), 58 Alta. L.R. (4th) 18 (C.A.). In Luscar Ltd. v. Smokey River Coal Ltd. (1999), 244 A.R. 196 (C.A.), Hunt J.A., in discussing leave to re-argue an appeal, said, at pp. 197–98: Those authorities make it clear that leave should not be granted lightly There must be a reason for the re-argument … Among the factors to be taken into account are whether there is a risk of a miscarriage of justice … whether the new arguments would affect the outcome … and whether the parties had the opportunity to address the issue in the original hearing … The Court of Appeal in Fas Gas Oil Ltd. v. J.H. Automotive Ltd. (2004), 31 Alta. L.R. (4th) 197 (C.A.) reiterated the law at p. 204: The principles summarized in Arrowhead have been confirmed by this Court on a number of occasions. … It is clear from these authorities that it is not sufficient to allege mere error; in order to be successful on an application for leave to re-argue, the error must have affected the result. Leave should not be granted lightly. …, and re-hearings should only be granted in exceptional circumstances; they should be discouraged. … The same point was made in 1368276 Alberta Ltd. v. Grotski, 2017 ABCA 230, 2017 CarswellAlta 1757 at paragraph 2. In Strichen v. Stewart (2005), 367 A.R. 188 (C.A.), Fruman J.A. said, at p. 190: The general test for leave to re-argue requires exceptional, special or unusual circumstances. This court has taken the position that re-hearings are to be discouraged: Portage Credit Union Ltd. v. D.E.R. Auctions Ltd. et al. (1994), 18 Alta. L.R. (3d) 185 (C.A.). When it is alleged that a court overlooked or misapprehended the evidence, the applicant must show that the overlooked or misapprehended evidence would have affected the outcome of the decision: Arrowhead Auto & Truck Parts Ltd. v. Calgary (City) (1997), 196 A.R. 57, 141 W.A.C. 57 (C.A.). In addition, the applicant must provide specific support for the allegation the court misled itself or was misled in considering the record before it, the nature of the issues or the questions to be addressed: Protestant School Board of Greater Montreal et al. v. Québec (Procureur général) et al., [1989] 2 S.C.R. 167, 97 N.R. 143, 25 Q.A.C. 118. In that case, the Supreme Court of Canada held that it was not reasonable to grant leave for a re-hearing simply because the applicant disagreed with certain findings. The appropriate recourse for such disagreements is to seek leave to appeal to a higher court; they are not grounds for a re-hearing: at p. 169. In Webb v. Birkett, 2011 ABCA 170, 2011 CarswellAlta 923, the Court said, at paragraphs 2–3: 2 Should leave to re-argue be given? Leave to re-argue should be granted in situations where the Court has been misled as regards to the record before it or the nature of the issues or the questions to be addressed: see Arrowhead Auto & Truck Parts Ltd. v. Calgary (City) (1997) 196 A.R. 57 at para. 3, referring to Greater Montreal Protestant School Board v. Quebec (Attorney General) [1989] 2 S.C.R. 167 at para. 3. The onus is on the applicant to show specific support for the suggestion the Court was mislead in relation to the record: see Strichen v. Stewart 2005 ABCA 201 at para. 6. 3 Further, leave may be granted “if it appears that the Court overlooked or misapprehended the evidence in a significant respect, and that a risk of miscarriage of justice ensued”: see Arrowhead at para. 3. However, a re-hearing is not meant to see if a panel member has changed his or her mind or to allow counsel to make arguments that might have been made on the original hearing of the appeal. In Toliver v. Koepke, 2013 ABCA 390, 2013 CarswellAlta 2267, 566 A.R. 24, the Court dismissed an application for leave to reargue an appeal, and said, at paragraphs 2–8: 2 Re-argument of an appeal is an extraordinary remedy that is not lightly granted. The purpose of re-argument is to address situations where the Court has been misled as regards to the record before it or the nature of the issues, or where it appears that the Court overlooked or misapprehended the evidence in a significant respect, or where patent errors are found in the decision or calculations: Webb v.
