The purpose of reargument is to address situations where the Court has been misled in regard to the record before it or the nature of the issues, or where it appears that the Court overlooked or misapprehended the evidence in a significant respect, or where patent errors are found in the decision or calculations: Webb v Birkett, 2011 ABCA 170 at paras.
2-3, 505 AR 311; Equitable Trust Co. v Lougheed Block Inc., 2012 ABCA 171 at para.
3, 533 AR 71; Toliver v Koepke, 2013 ABCA 390, 566 AR 24 additional reasons at 2013 ABCA 398, 566 AR 27.

A rehearing is not meant to allow counsel to make or remake arguments that might have been or were made on the original hearing of the appeal: Keller (Next friend of) v Penkoske, 2004 ABCA 267 at para.
5; Watts Estate v Contact Canada Tourism Services Ltd., 2001 ABCA 135 at para.
8, 281 AR 290. … In McLelland v.
McLelland, 2021 ABCA 238, 2021 CarswellAlta 1527, 67 E.T.R.
(4th) 1, the Court said: [2] The purpose of reopening an appeal is to address situations where:
(a) the Court has been misled about the record or the issues
(b) it appears that the Court has overlooked or misapprehended the evidence in a significant respect; or
(c) patent errors are found in the decision or calculations: WestJet v ELS Marketing Inc., 2014 ABCA 372 at para 3, 13 Alta LR

The purpose is not to allow the losing party to reargue the appeal or to advance additional arguments that might have been made in the original hearing: Doe v Alberta, 2014 ABCA 246 at para 3, 69 CPC (7th) 44; WestJet at para 3.
There is a “heavy onus” on the applicant to justify a rehearing: Angus v R Angus Alberta Ltd (1988), 1988 ABCA 279 (CanLII), 62 Alta LR (2d) 33 at 34 (CA).
To succeed, an applicant must show that the error would have affected the result: Keller v Penkoske, 2004 ABCA 267.
[3] The Court has inherent jurisdiction to control and regulate its own process to set aside entry of a judgment or order that has been improperly entered.
However, its power to do so is narrow and discretionary, and will only be exercised if: “(1) there has been no delay in applying
(2) no party has taken the benefit of the judgment or order
(3) no party will suffer prejudice as a result of setting aside entry of the judgment or order and permitting the application for leave to proceed on its merits; and
(4) the interests of justice favour setting aside entry”: Fas Gas Oil Ltd v JH Automotive Ltd, 2004 ABCA 120 at paras 19, 25-26, 348 AR 65. … 3.
Summarily Disposing of an Issue in an Appeal In CCS Corporation v.
Pembina Pipeline Corporation, 2017 ABCA 260, 2017 CarswellAlta 1418, Justice Slatter said: 8 … Further, apart from the narrow circumstances set out in R.
14.74, the Court of Appeal does not have any procedure for the “summary determination” of appeals: Boyd v Alberta (Workers' Compensation Board), 2015 ABCA 191 at para.
9 The resources required to summarily decide an appeal are virtually identical to the resources required to simply argue the appeal in the normal way.

Under both procedures both parties would have to file written argument (factums or memoranda); three judges of the Court would have to read the trial reasons, the factums, other portions of the record and the authorities; time would have to be devoted for oral argument; and reasons for decision would have to be prepared.
Further, if the answer to this one issue did not resolve the dispute, there would potentially have to be a full argument of the other issues raised in the appeal in any event.
It is rarely in the interests of justice to decide appeals piecemeal, or to attempt to summarily dispose of them.
Rule 14.38(2)(d)—when it does not apply In Waquan v.
Canada (Attorney General), 2021 ABCA 212, 2021 CarswellAlta 1389, the Court of Appeal had previously set aside, in part, an order striking out a statement of claim.

The judgment roll set out the claims which could proceed, and stated “those Plaintiffs are at liberty to amend the Claim to particularize such claims.” The plaintiffs subsequently filed an amended statement of claim, but the defendants were of the view that the amended statement of claim did not comply with the Court of Appeal's ruling.
The defendants brought an application under R.
14.38(2)(d) “for an order directing the plaintiffs to amend their statement of claim” so that it complied with the defendants' understanding of the Court of Appeal earlier ruling.
The Court of Appeal said that R.
14.38(2)(b) did not apply.

The Court said: [4] A threshold issue is whether this application is contemplated by Rule 14.38(2)(d) or whether it is more appropriately dealt with by the case management judge in the Court of Queen's Bench.
This action has been case managed since April 2015, first by former Chief Justice Wittmann until his retirement in 2018, and since by Associate Chief Justice Rooke.
[5] Our decision was an adjudication of the types of claims which should be allowed to proceed and which should be struck.
It did not direct the plaintiffs as to the specific manner in which to plead their case.
This is typical of an appeal involving whether to strike claims based upon the pleadings.

We note the recent decision in PricewaterhouseCoopers Inc v Perpetual Energy Inc., 2021 ABCA 16 where this court allowed an appeal of a case management judge's decision to strike certain claims from the statement of claim.
The court granted leave to amend the statement of claim and directed that any disputes about the pleadings be resolved by the case management judge: PricewaterhouseCoopers at para 227.
[6] This is a dispute about pleadings, something which is within the purview of the trial court.
Were it otherwise, this court would become the arbiter of every dispute about a pleading which arose from an appeal involving striking or amending a pleading.
We are not persuaded that Rule 14.38(2)(d) was intended to have this effect.
[7] In sum, we conclude that this is not the type of application for directions contemplated by Rule 14.38(2)(d).
The parties are directed to the Court of Queen's Bench case management judge to resolve the defendants' concerns with the amended statement of claim.
The application is dismissed.
